schlacht-am-bach-dang-938#text: Since 111 BC Chinese dynasties had ruled the Red River Delta, and there had been repeated uprisings, for example under the Trưng sisters. When, after the end of the Tang dynasty, the Southern Han kingdom sent a fleet, Ngô Quyền had iron-tipped stakes driven into the riverbed at the mouth of the Bạch Đằng. At high tide he lured the ships over them; at low tide they were impaled and destroyed, and the enemy prince was killed. In 939 Ngô Quyền made himself king. After years of internal fighting Đinh Bộ Lĩnh united the country in 968, in 1010 Thăng Long, today's Hanoi, became the capital, and from 1054 the state was called Đại Việt. Using the same stake tactic, Trần Hưng Đạo defeated the Mongols on the Bạch Đằng in 1288.
runenstein-von-jelling#title: Harald Bluetooth and the Jelling Runestone
runenstein-von-jelling#summary: The Danish king Harald Bluetooth is baptized and erects a runestone at Jelling that praises him as the unifier of Denmark and converter of the Danes.
runenstein-von-jelling#text: Around 965, according to the Saxon chronicler Widukind, Harald Bluetooth accepted Christianity after a cleric named Poppo is said to have passed an ordeal by fire. At Jelling he had a great runestone set up in honour of his parents Gorm and Thyra, whose inscription names him as the Harald “who won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian”. The stone bears one of the oldest depictions of Christ in Scandinavia and is called “Denmark’s baptismal certificate”. The burial mounds, stones and church of Jelling are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
erik-der-rote-besiedelt-groenland#summar: Erik the Red, banished from Iceland, leads settlers to Greenland, where two Norse settlements arise that last more than 450 years.
erik-der-rote-besiedelt-groenland#text: Erik the Red had been banished from Iceland for three years for killings and used this time to explore the west coast of Greenland. Around 985 or 986, according to the sagas, he returned with some 25 ships, of which only 14 arrived. He is said to have chosen the name “Green Land” to attract settlers. The Eastern and Western Settlements arose, with farms, churches and later a bishop’s seat; the inhabitants lived from livestock, seal hunting and the trade in walrus ivory. The Western Settlement was abandoned in the 14th century and the Eastern Settlement in the 15th; the reasons are debated.
besiedlung-ostpolynesiens#summary: In an astonishingly rapid expansion, Polynesian voyagers reach the Society Islands, the Marquesas, Hawaiʻi and Rapa Nui.
besiedlung-ostpolynesiens#text: After the long pause in West Polynesia, seafarers pushed east from about the 10th or 11th century. Recent radiocarbon dating suggests that the Society Islands were settled around 1000 to 1100 and the most remote islands within about two centuries, among them Hawaiʻi in the north and Rapa Nui in the southeast; older research had assumed considerably earlier dates. The settlers brought taro, breadfruit, coconut palms, pigs, dogs and chickens, though not every species reached every island. Finds of the sweet potato, which originated in South America, and genetic studies point to contacts with South America; how and when they happened is disputed.
island-nimmt-das-christentum-an#summary: To avoid a civil war between pagans and Christians, the Althing decides that all Icelanders are to become Christians.
island-nimmt-das-christentum-an#text: Under pressure from the Norwegian king Olaf Tryggvason, who was holding Icelanders in Norway as hostages, Christians and followers of the old gods faced each other in hostility at the Althing around 1000. Both sides left the decision to the lawspeaker Þorgeir, himself a pagan. After a day and a night of reflection he announced that all Icelanders must be baptized, for one land needed one law. For a transitional period sacrifices in private and old customs such as the exposure of infants remained permitted. Peaceful adoption by decision of an assembly is regarded as unique in Europe.
leif-eriksson-erreicht-vinland#summary: Around 1000 Leif Eriksson sails west from Greenland and becomes one of the first Europeans to reach North America.
leif-eriksson-erreicht-vinland#text: According to the Saga of the Greenlanders and Erik the Red’s Saga, Leif Eriksson discovered on his voyage the lands of Helluland (“Land of Flat Stones”), Markland (“Forest Land”) and Vinland, where he spent the winter; Baffin Island, Labrador and areas around the Gulf of St. Lawrence are probably meant. Further voyages followed, including an attempt at settlement by Thorfinn Karlsefni and Gudrid, which was abandoned after conflicts with the local people, called Skrælings in the sagas. In 1960 Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the remains of Norse buildings at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland; wood from the site has been dated precisely to the year 1021. Whether L’Anse aux Meadows itself was Vinland is debated.
schlacht-bei-svolder#summary: The Norwegian king Olaf Tryggvason is defeated by an alliance of Danes, Swedes and Norwegian opponents and dies in the sea battle.
schlacht-bei-svolder#text: Olaf Tryggvason had ruled Norway since 995 and spread Christianity by force. Around 1000 the Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard, the Swedish king Olof Skötkonung and the Norwegian jarl Eric Haakonsson confronted him with their fleets. Where the battle took place is unknown; the Øresund or the waters near Rügen have been suggested. According to tradition, when his ship the “Long Serpent” was taken, Olaf leapt overboard in full armour. Norway was then divided among the victors.
schlacht-am-kleidion#summary: Basil II defeats the army of the Bulgarian tsar Samuel and decides a war that had lasted decades.
schlacht-am-kleidion#text: On 29 July 1014 Byzantine troops outflanked the Bulgarian barricades in the Kleidion pass, in what is now southwestern Bulgaria, and routed their army. According to the chronicler John Skylitzes, Basil II had some 15,000 prisoners blinded and sent them back to Samuel, with one one-eyed man leading every hundred; at the sight of them Samuel is said to have suffered a fatal stroke. The numbers are probably exaggerated. By 1018 Bulgaria had been fully incorporated into the empire. Basil later received the epithet "Bulgar-slayer".
knut-wird-koenig-von-england#title: Cnut the Great Becomes King of England
knut-wird-koenig-von-england#summary: After the death of Edmund Ironside the Dane Cnut becomes king of all England and over the following years builds up a North Sea Empire.
knut-wird-koenig-von-england#text: Cnut’s father Sweyn Forkbeard had conquered England in 1013 but died in 1014. Cnut returned with an army in 1015, defeated Edmund Ironside at Assandun in 1016 and after Edmund’s death in November became king of all England. He married Emma of Normandy, the widow of King Æthelred, and governed with Anglo-Saxon and Danish magnates. In 1018 or 1019 he inherited Denmark, and in 1028 he won Norway. His North Sea Empire quickly fell apart after his death in 1035; in 1042 the Anglo-Saxon royal house returned in England with Edward the Confessor.
jaroslaw-der-weise-und-die-russkaja-praw: Yaroslav the Wise and the Russkaya Pravda
Under Grand Prince Yaroslav, Kyiv enjoys its golden age; the law code Russkaya Pravda sets down the law of the Rus in writing for the first time.

After a bloody war between brothers, Yaroslav prevailed in Kyiv in 1019 and ruled until his death in 1054. He fortified the city with the Golden Gate and, according to the chronicle, founded St Sophia's Cathedral in 1037, whose mosaics and frescoes survive to this day. The oldest version of the Russkaya Pravda, the first law code of the Rus, goes back to him: it limited blood feud and set fines for killing, injury and theft; his sons expanded it. Through the marriages of his daughters to the kings of France, Norway and Hungary, Kyiv was closely tied to the rest of Europe. After Yaroslav's death the Rus increasingly fragmented into appanage principalities.
schlacht-bei-stiklestad#summary: King Olaf Haraldsson falls fighting Norwegian peasant armies; soon afterwards he is venerated as a saint and becomes Norway’s patron.
schlacht-bei-stiklestad#text: Olaf Haraldsson had united Norway from 1015 and imposed Christianity harshly, but in 1028 he fled to Kiev from Cnut the Great and discontented magnates. On his return a superior army confronted him at Stiklestad on 29 July 1030, and he was killed. As early as 1031 his body was exhumed and venerated as a relic in Nidaros, today’s Trondheim; reports of miracles made him “Norway’s eternal king”. His tomb in Nidaros Cathedral became one of the most important pilgrimage destinations in northern Europe.
anawrahta-eint-pagan#title: Anawrahta Unites the Kingdom of Pagan
anawrahta-eint-pagan#summary: Under King Anawrahta, Pagan on the Irrawaddy becomes the centre of the first kingdom to unite large parts of present-day Myanmar.
anawrahta-eint-pagan#text: Anawrahta came to the throne of the principality of Pagan in central Burma in 1044 and subjugated many neighbouring areas in the following decades. According to tradition he conquered the Mon city of Thaton in 1057 and brought monks, craftsmen and sacred texts of Theravada Buddhism from there to Pagan. Under him and successors such as Kyanzittha, more than 10,000 temples, stupas and monasteries were built on the plain beside the Irrawaddy, of which over 2,000 still survive. Pagan became a centre of Theravada Buddhism in close contact with Sri Lanka. After Mongol attacks at the end of the 13th century the kingdom broke up into several realms.
morgenlaendisches-schisma#summary: Papal legates and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other; the year has become a symbol of the split between the Eastern and Western churches.
morgenlaendisches-schisma#text: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida laid a bull of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of the Hagia Sophia, whereupon the patriarch excommunicated the legates in turn. The disputes concerned papal primacy, the Filioque in the Creed and customs such as the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. Historians today see the separation as a long process that was sealed only by the Crusades and the sack of Constantinople in 1204. Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the mutual excommunications in 1965.
schlacht-bei-stamford-bridge#summary: The English king Harold Godwinson defeats a Norwegian invasion army near York; King Harald Hardrada falls and the Viking Age comes to an end.
schlacht-bei-stamford-bridge#text: After the death of Edward the Confessor early in 1066, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada claimed England and in September landed in the north with Tostig, the exiled brother of the new king Harold Godwinson. After a victory at Fulford the Norwegians were surprised at Stamford Bridge on 25 September by the English army, which had arrived by forced marches; Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed. Only three days later William of Normandy landed in the south, and on 14 October Harold Godwinson was defeated at Hastings. Stamford Bridge is regarded as the end of the Viking Age.
alexios-komnenos-wird-kaiser#summary: A general from the aristocratic House of Komnenos takes over the weakened empire and rescues it from a severe crisis.
alexios-komnenos-wird-kaiser#text: After Manzikert in 1071 the Seljuks had occupied large parts of Asia Minor, in the west the Normans under Robert Guiscard were attacking, and civil wars paralysed the empire. Alexios I Komnenos seized power in 1081, fought off the Normans with Venetian help and defeated the Pechenegs in 1091. His request for Western mercenaries contributed to Pope Urban II's call for the First Crusade in 1095. With the crusaders he recovered parts of Asia Minor, but relations with them remained marked by mistrust, as the Alexiad by his daughter Anna Komnene shows.
handelsprivileg-fuer-venedig#summary: In return for naval help against the Normans, the Venetians receive the right to trade duty-free throughout the empire.
handelsprivileg-fuer-venedig#text: Alexios I needed the Venetian fleet against the Normans and granted Venice far-reaching privileges in a gold-sealed charter, a chrysobull: Venetian merchants were allowed to trade in almost all ports of the empire without paying duties and received their own quarter with landing stages on the Golden Horn. The charter is usually dated to 1082, though some historians place it in 1092. The privilege made Venice rich and powerful but weakened Byzantine merchants and state revenues; later Pisa and Genoa also received similar rights.
erzbistum-lund#title: Lund Becomes the Archbishopric of the North
erzbistum-lund#summary: The pope raises Lund, then Danish, to the seat of an archbishop for all Scandinavia; the Nordic church separates from Hamburg-Bremen.
erzbistum-lund#text: Until the early 12th century the dioceses of Scandinavia were subject to the archbishopric of Hamburg-Bremen, which the Nordic kings increasingly resented. At the instigation of the Danish king Eric Ejegod, the pope established an archbishopric for the whole North in 1103 or 1104 at Lund in Scania, then part of Denmark. In 1152/53 Norway received its own archbishopric at Nidaros, and in 1164 Sweden at Uppsala. Construction of Lund’s Romanesque cathedral began at this time, and it is one of the most important church buildings in Scandinavia.
schlacht-von-myriokephalon#summary: Emperor Manuel I Komnenos suffers a defeat against the Seljuks that ends hopes of recovering Asia Minor.
schlacht-von-myriokephalon#text: In 1176 Manuel I marched with a large army against Konya, the capital of the Seljuks of Rum under Sultan Kılıç Arslan II. In a narrow pass near Myriokephalon in western Anatolia the column was ambushed and suffered heavy losses. Although Manuel was able to negotiate a peace and lead his army back, he is said to have compared the defeat himself to Manzikert. Afterwards Byzantium gave up its plan to reconquer the interior of Asia Minor.
jayavarman-vii-und-angkor-thom#summary: After driving out the Cham, Jayavarman VII becomes king of the Khmer and builds Angkor Thom with the Bayon as his new capital.
jayavarman-vii-und-angkor-thom#text: In 1177 troops from Champa had sacked Angkor. Jayavarman VII drove out the invaders and was crowned in 1181. A devout Mahayana Buddhist, he built the fortified city of Angkor Thom with walls almost three kilometres long, at whose centre stands the Bayon with its many towers covered in huge stone faces. He added temple monasteries such as Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, which he dedicated to his mother and his father. According to his inscriptions he founded more than a hundred hospitals and numerous rest houses along the roads. Under him the Khmer Empire reached its greatest extent, but the enormous building effort placed a heavy burden on the country.
tui-tonga-reich#title: Height of the Tuʻi Tonga empire
tui-tonga-reich#summary: The sacred kings of Tonga, the Tuʻi Tonga, gain influence far beyond their own islands.
tui-tonga-reich#text: According to tradition, ʻAhoʻeitu, a son of the sky god Tangaloa, founded the Tuʻi Tonga line in the 10th century. From their seat at Lapaha on Tongatapu, where large stone tombs known as langi survive, the rulers gained influence over neighbouring island groups in roughly the 12th and 13th centuries; how far this "empire" actually extended is disputed among scholars. The stone trilithon Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, built around 1200, is attributed to the Tuʻi Tonga Tuʻitātui. In the 15th century the Tuʻi Tonga transferred secular power to a second line, the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, and remained above all spiritual leaders.
pluenderung-konstantinopels-1204#summary: The army of the Fourth Crusade captures the Christian capital and sets up a Latin Empire.
pluenderung-konstantinopels-1204#text: The Fourth Crusade was actually meant to go to Egypt, but the crusaders were deeply in debt to Venice. Under the influence of Doge Enrico Dandolo they first moved against Zara and then on to Constantinople to install a claimant to the throne who had promised them large payments. When the money failed to materialize, they stormed the city on 13 April 1204 and plundered it for days; church treasures, relics and the bronze horses from the Hippodrome were carried off to the West. Baldwin of Flanders became emperor of the Latin Empire, Venice secured ports and islands, and Greeks founded rival states in Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond.
gruendung-des-franziskanerordens#title: The Founding of the Franciscan Order
gruendung-des-franziskanerordens#summary: Pope Innocent III gives verbal approval to the way of life of Francis of Assisi and his companions; the first great mendicant order is born.
gruendung-des-franziskanerordens#text: Around 1209 or 1210 Francis travelled to Rome with a few companions and received permission from Innocent III to live in poverty and to preach. Unlike the monks of the old orders, the Friars Minor did not live in seclusion on landed estates but without possessions in the growing towns, where they preached and cared for the poor and sick. In 1223 Pope Honorius III confirmed the final rule. Together with the Dominicans, the Franciscans shaped pastoral care, universities and missions in the late Middle Ages; the question of how strictly poverty should be observed, however, soon led to bitter conflict within the order.
schlacht-bei-las-navas-de-tolosa#title: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
schlacht-bei-las-navas-de-tolosa#summary: An alliance of Christian kings of Spain defeats the army of the Almohads; the Reconquista gains decisive momentum.
schlacht-bei-las-navas-de-tolosa#text: On 16 July 1212 King Alfonso VIII of Castile, Peter II of Aragon and Sancho VII of Navarre, supported by knights from Portugal and France, defeated the army of the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir in the Sierra Morena. Pope Innocent III had declared the campaign a crusade. The defeat decisively weakened Almohad rule in al-Andalus. In the following decades Castile and Aragon conquered Córdoba (1236), Valencia (1238) and Seville (1248); only the Emirate of Granada remained Muslim until 1492.
snorri-schreibt-die-edda#title: Snorri Sturluson Writes the Prose Edda
snorri-schreibt-die-edda#summary: The Icelandic scholar Snorri Sturluson writes a handbook of poetry that becomes the most important source on the Norse gods.
snorri-schreibt-die-edda#text: Around 1220 Snorri Sturluson wrote the Snorra Edda or Prose Edda, named after him. It was meant to explain to young poets the old images and circumlocutions of skaldic poetry, and to this end it tells the myths of the creation of the world, of Odin, Thor and Loki, down to the end of the world, Ragnarök. As a Christian, Snorri interpreted the gods as deified humans of ancient times. There is also the Poetic Edda, a collection of older poems about gods and heroes preserved above all in a manuscript from around 1270, the Codex Regius.
gruendung-von-sukhothai#title: Founding of the Kingdom of Sukhothai
gruendung-von-sukhothai#summary: Thai chiefs drive out the Khmer governor and found Sukhothai, which Thailand regards as the cradle of its nation.
gruendung-von-sukhothai#text: According to tradition, around 1238 two Thai chiefs freed the city of Sukhothai from Khmer overlordship; one of them became its first king as Si Inthrathit. Under King Ramkhamhaeng in the late 13th century Sukhothai's influence spread widely, and Theravada Buddhism became the state religion. A stone inscription of 1292 praises the king as a just ruler and is associated with the creation of the Thai script; its authenticity, however, is disputed. Sukhothai was also known for glazed ceramics that were traded as far as Indonesia and Japan. From the 14th century it came under the influence of Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, into which it was absorbed in 1438.
eisschlacht-auf-dem-peipussee#summary: Prince Alexander Nevsky and troops from Novgorod defeat an army of the Livonian Order on frozen Lake Peipus.
eisschlacht-auf-dem-peipussee#text: While the Mongols were devastating the south of the Rus, Swedes and the knights of the Livonian Order, a branch of the Teutonic Order, advanced from the west. Alexander, prince of Novgorod, defeated the Swedes on the Neva in 1240, which earned him his byname, and recaptured the town of Pskov, which the knights had occupied. On 5 April 1242 he defeated an army of the Order and the bishops on the ice of Lake Peipus. By today's estimates the number of combatants was rather small; the clash became a great decisive battle above all in later memory, for instance in Sergei Eisenstein's film of 1938. The border between the Orthodox Rus and the Catholic Baltic remained stable for a long time afterwards.
moai-auf-rapa-nui#summary: The inhabitants of Easter Island carve hundreds of stone figures that are erected on platforms along the coast.
moai-auf-rapa-nui#text: On Rapa Nui, one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, the inhabitants created almost 900 large stone figures, the moai, from roughly the 13th to the 16th century. Most were carved from the tuff of the Rano Raraku crater, and many were set up on ceremonial platforms, the ahu, with their backs to the sea. They are regarded as representations of revered ancestors whose mana was meant to protect the community. How the figures were transported, and whether island society collapsed through deforestation even before Europeans arrived, is disputed; recent research tends to emphasize the devastating effects of introduced diseases and the Peruvian slave raids of 1862/63.
besiedlung-neuseelands#summary: New Zealand, the last large landmass on Earth to be settled, is reached by East Polynesian voyagers whose descendants are the Māori.
besiedlung-neuseelands#text: Radiocarbon dates, volcanic ash layers and finds such as the introduced Pacific rat show that settlers from East Polynesia, probably from the Society or Cook Islands, reached New Zealand around 1250 to 1300. Māori tradition tells of Hawaiki as the homeland and of canoes such as Tainui, Te Arawa and Aotea, to which the tribes still trace their origins. The settlers found a cooler land in which tropical plants barely grew; they hunted seals and the large flightless moa, which were wiped out within roughly one to two centuries. By about 1500 the distinct culture of the Māori had developed from its East Polynesian roots.
rueckeroberung-konstantinopels-1261#summ: Troops of the emperor of Nicaea take Constantinople and bring the Latin Empire to an end.
rueckeroberung-konstantinopels-1261#text: In July 1261 troops under the general Alexios Strategopoulos entered the city almost without a fight while the Venetian fleet was away; the Latin emperor Baldwin II fled. Michael VIII Palaiologos made a solemn entry in August and was crowned in the Hagia Sophia. Beforehand he had promised Genoa far-reaching trading rights in the Treaty of Nymphaeum. The restored empire was impoverished and reduced in size, but the Palaiologan dynasty ruled for almost two centuries until 1453.
island-unterwirft-sich-norwegen#title: Iceland Submits to the Norwegian King
island-unterwirft-sich-norwegen#summary: After decades of bloody power struggles between the great families, the Icelanders swear allegiance to King Haakon IV of Norway; the Commonwealth ends.
island-unterwirft-sich-norwegen#text: In the 13th century, the Age of the Sturlungs, a few powerful families fought for control of Iceland, and the Norwegian king Haakon IV used the feuds to gain influence. Between 1262 and 1264 the Icelanders recognized the king as their ruler in the Old Covenant (Gamli sáttmáli); in return he promised peace, Icelandic law and regular sailings. Greenland had already submitted in 1261. The Althing continued to exist but lost its role as legislator. Together with Norway, Iceland came under Danish rule in 1380 and became an independent republic only in 1944.
gruendung-von-majapahit#summary: Raden Wijaya uses a Mongol punitive expedition against Java to defeat his rivals and founds the kingdom of Majapahit.
gruendung-von-majapahit#text: The ruler of Singhasari in East Java had rebuffed envoys of Kublai Khan and was killed by a rival in 1292. When a Yuan dynasty fleet landed on Java in 1293, his son-in-law Raden Wijaya allied with it, defeated the rival and then drove out the Mongols. His new capital Majapahit lay near present-day Trowulan. Under the minister Gajah Mada and King Hayam Wuruk the kingdom reached its height in the 14th century; the poem Nagarakretagama of 1365 lists places across the whole archipelago as dependencies, although how firm this rule was is disputed. In the 15th century Majapahit lost power to the rising Muslim coastal states and came to an end in the early 16th century.
islam-in-samudera-pasai#title: The Spread of Islam: Samudera Pasai
islam-in-samudera-pasai#summary: In northern Sumatra Samudera Pasai emerges as one of the first Islamic sultanates in Southeast Asia; from the ports Islam spreads across the archipelago.
islam-in-samudera-pasai#text: Muslim merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and China had long been visitors to the ports of Southeast Asia. Marco Polo reported Muslims at Perlak on Sumatra in 1292, and the gravestone of Sultan Malik al-Salih of Samudera Pasai, dated 1297, is regarded as early evidence of an Islamic ruler in the region. Ibn Battuta visited Pasai around 1345 and described a pious and learned sultan. Islam spread mainly through trade, marriage, scholars and Sufis, hardly through conquest. After Malacca around 1400, the ports on Java's north coast, Brunei, Aceh, Makassar and the sultanates of Sulu and Mindanao converted to Islam; today Indonesia is the country with the largest Muslim population in the world.
aufstieg-moskaus-unter-iwan-kalita#title: The Rise of Moscow under Ivan Kalita
aufstieg-moskaus-unter-iwan-kalita#summa: Prince Ivan I wins the favour of the Golden Horde, draws the metropolitan to Moscow and lays the foundation for the city's rise.
aufstieg-moskaus-unter-iwan-kalita#text: Moscow, first mentioned in 1147, was long a small princely seat in the shadow of Vladimir and Tver. Ivan I, known as Kalita, "Moneybag", helped the Horde suppress an uprising in Tver in 1327 and in return received the office of grand prince and the right to collect the tribute of the other princes. At the very beginning of his reign Metropolitan Peter, the head of the Russian church, had moved his seat to Moscow, where he died and was buried in 1326. Ivan bought up estates and villages and so enlarged his principality. The church, money and cooperation with the Horde made Moscow the strongest principality of the north-eastern Rus.
goldene-bulle-karls-iv#summary: Emperor Charles IV lays down in an imperial law that seven prince-electors choose the king of the Romans by majority vote.
goldene-bulle-karls-iv#text: After decades of disputed double elections, Charles IV issued the Golden Bull, named after its golden seal, at the imperial diets of Nuremberg and Metz in 1356. It named the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, the king of Bohemia, the count palatine of the Rhine, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg as electors, who were to elect the king in Frankfurt by majority; no confirmation by the pope was provided for. The electorates could not be divided, and their holders received far-reaching rights. The Golden Bull remained the most important fundamental law of the Holy Roman Empire until its end in 1806.
waldemar-erobert-visby#summary: The Danish king Valdemar IV Atterdag conquers Gotland and the rich trading town of Visby, triggering war with the Hanseatic League.
waldemar-erobert-visby#text: In the summer of 1361 Valdemar IV landed on Gotland with an army and defeated a levy of Gotland peasants before the walls of Visby; mass graves with more than a thousand dead were found in excavations in the 20th century. The town surrendered and had to pay a large indemnity, though the legend of a ransom paid in barrels of silver is a later embellishment. Because Valdemar had also recovered Scania and made the passage through the Øresund more expensive for Hanseatic merchants, the Hanseatic towns joined forces against him in the Confederation of Cologne in 1367.
frieden-von-stralsund#summary: After its victory over Denmark the Hanseatic League secures trading privileges and, for 15 years, the castles on the coast of Scania in the Peace of Stralsund.
frieden-von-stralsund#text: The Hanseatic towns allied in the Confederation of Cologne and their partners ravaged the Danish coasts in 1368/69 and took Copenhagen and the castles of Scania. In the Peace of Stralsund of 24 May 1370 Denmark had to confirm free trade and low tolls for the merchants and leave them the most important fortresses on the Øresund, together with their revenues, for 15 years. The peace is regarded as the high point of the political power of the Hanseatic League. Valdemar IV died in 1375; his daughter Margaret then secured the throne for her son Olaf.
